CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain with referral for evaluation of esophagitis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a new patient with a referral from the emergency room for evaluation of esophagitis. She reports that approximately three months ago in early October 2020, she developed sudden onset chest pain located in the center of her chest behind the breastbone. The pain was sharp and felt like she was having a heart attack. It occurred randomly and lasted for four days, during which nothing she tried relieved it. The pain was worse with eating. She also noted associated difficulty swallowing during this time. After four days, she went to the emergency room where she underwent EKG and blood tests, which were all normal. The cardiac workup was unremarkable. The chest pain and swallowing difficulties resolved approximately three days after the ER visit. She has been asymptomatic for the past three months since the initial episode. She reports this occurred during a stressful job transition. She denies abdominal pain, and bowel movements are normal. She has been trying to lose weight.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies current chest pain. Denies abdominal pain. Bowel movements normal. No other concerning symptoms reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Uterine fibroids
Anemia
Cholecystectomy several years ago

MEDICATIONS
Not documented in visit.

ALLERGIES
Not documented in visit.

FAMILY HISTORY
Denies family history of gastrointestinal problems.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Currently employed; was undergoing a stressful job transition around the time of symptom onset.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Soft. Lower abdomen non-tender to palpation. Mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants bilaterally, approximately equal on left and right. No acute distress.

RESULTS
EKG (from ER): Normal
Blood tests (from ER): Normal
Cardiac workup: Normal

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Chest pain with associated dysphagia, resolved. Differential diagnosis includes GERD, dyspepsia, esophagitis, musculoskeletal etiologies, and anxiety. Most likely etiology is anxiety-related chest pain secondary to recent job transition, with possible musculoskeletal contribution and/or transient reflux esophagitis. Given resolution of symptoms three months ago and prolonged asymptomatic period, esophagitis likely already healed. Discussed upper endoscopy (EGD) versus conservative management with monitoring. Patient elected to self-monitor for symptom recurrence. Will call office if experiences additional episodes of pain or other concerning symptoms, at which time EGD can be scheduled. Otherwise, follow up as needed for any other GI complaints.
